analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee for the rest of the 112th Congress after one subcommittee hearing, leaving private student loans as hard to erase in bankruptcy as ever.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal bankruptcy law, almost no student loan can be canceled even when a borrower has no realistic way to pay, unless the borrower can prove the debt would cause an "undue hardship" — a standard most people cannot meet. This bill would have changed that only for loans from private lenders, letting people who file for bankruptcy treat those debts like credit card or medical bills, while keeping government-backed loans protected.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose finances were wrecked by private student loans and who ended up in bankruptcy — disproportionately borrowers who left school without finishing, attended for-profit colleges, or fell into long-term unemployment. For them, the bill offered a way to restart instead of carrying an unpayable debt for life.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers with unpayable private student loans

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the federal bankruptcy code so that loans from private lenders are no longer automatically exempt from being canceled in bankruptcy; they would be treated like other consumer debt. [S2]
Loans made, insured, or guaranteed by a government — federal student loans — would remain protected from discharge, so the change is aimed squarely at private-market loans. [S3]

Private student loans typically carry higher interest rates and fewer borrower protections than federal loans, and today a borrower must win an "undue hardship" lawsuit inside the bankruptcy case to erase them — a standard courts apply so strictly that very few succeed. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan companies and any banks that hold these loans would absorb losses when borrowers canceled debts in bankruptcy, and lenders would likely price that risk into higher rates or tighter underwriting for future student loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private student loan companies and banks

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only private loans, leaving the far larger population of borrowers struggling with federal student loans under the same harsh "undue hardship" standard. [S3]

Lenders would face higher expected losses on private student loans, which could mean higher interest rates or fewer loans extended to students with weak credit — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge. [S2]
Opening bankruptcy discharge to student debt could increase bankruptcy filings and, some argued, shift costs from borrowers to lenders and their investors. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers the bill reached — people drowning in private student loans — the benefit was substantial: the same fresh start in bankruptcy that every other kind of consumer debt already allows. The main cost falls on lenders and shows up in loan pricing, not on the general public. The bill's biggest honest weakness is how narrow it is: federal loans, where most student debt sits, stay untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill once and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which held a single subcommittee hearing and then let it die without ever voting to send it to the full Senate.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on May 26, 2011, with Senators Franken and Whitehouse, and the Senate referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary. [S1]
Six Democratic senators added their names as cosponsors; no Republican did. [S4]
On March 20, 2012, a Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on the bill — the only action the committee took during the two-year Congress. [S5]
The committee never voted to report the bill, so it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan companies came out ahead: because the bill died in committee, their loans kept the special protection that makes them almost impossible to erase in bankruptcy, preserving their ability to collect from borrowers even after bankruptcy. Struggling borrowers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks supporting it.

for.name: Sens. Al Franken and Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Joined Durbin in introducing the bill on day one.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held one subcommittee hearing and never voted the bill out of committee, keeping it off the Senate floor.

against.name: Private student loan industry
against.role: Lenders and servicers of private student loans
against.what_they_did: Opposed making private student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy, which would have allowed borrowers to erase these debts and cost lenders money.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill also never attracted a floor vote, so there was no roll call to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped away the bankruptcy protection that makes private student loans nearly impossible to cancel, exposing lenders to losses when borrowers' finances collapse. Because the bill died, lenders kept that protection and kept collecting from borrowers even after bankruptcy.
Government-backed student loans would remain protected from discharge, so the bill leaves the federal loan program's special status fully intact while only freeing private-market loans.
